h1: Talking to your teen about mental health
p: Starting the conversation can feel awkward for everyone. A few thoughtful approaches can help your teen feel heard, not lectured.
The Journal · Notes from our therapists
Teens often want to be understood more than advised. If you’re worried about your child’s mood, sleep or withdrawal, knowing how to open the door can make all the difference.

Choose low-pressure moments — car rides, walks or cooking together — rather than a formal sit-down. Lead with curiosity: “You’ve seemed tired lately, how are things really?” Then listen more than you speak, and resist the urge to fix things straight away.

If changes last more than a couple of weeks or begin to affect school, friendships or safety, it’s a good time to involve a professional. Family therapy can also help everyone communicate with a little more ease.

h1: Anxiety, explained: why your body sounds the alarm
h2: The alarm system behind the feeling
p: Racing heart, tight chest, spiralling thoughts. Understanding what anxiety is actually doing can make it feel a lot less frightening.
The Journal · Notes from our therapists

Anxiety can feel like it comes out of nowhere: a pounding heart in a quiet room, a knot in your stomach before an ordinary meeting. But your body isn’t malfunctioning. It’s trying, a little too hard, to keep you safe.

When your brain senses a threat, it triggers the fight-or-flight response. Breathing quickens, muscles tense and your attention narrows. That response is brilliant in real danger, but it can switch on for deadlines, conversations or even memories — and then struggle to switch off.

Slow exhales, naming what you can see and hear, and gently questioning anxious predictions all signal to your nervous system that you’re okay. In therapy, we build on these skills and look at what keeps the alarm so sensitive in the first place.

h1: Five small habits for a calmer nervous system
p: You don’t need a retreat to feel steadier. These tiny, repeatable rituals help your body remember what safe feels like.
The Journal · Notes from our therapists
Feeling calmer rarely comes from one big change. More often, it’s built from small moments that tell your nervous system it can rest. Here are five you can start today, no special equipment required.

Step outside for a few minutes of daylight each morning. Try a longer out-breath than in-breath. Put your phone in another room for the first and last half hour of the day. Move your body in a way that feels kind, not punishing. And end the day by noticing one thing that went okay.
Missing a day doesn’t undo your progress. The goal isn’t a flawless routine — it’s a gentler relationship with yourself, practised a little at a time.

h1: Fighting fair: how couples can repair after conflict
p: Every relationship has rupture. What matters most is how you come back together — and it’s a skill you can learn.
The Journal · Notes from our therapists

Every couple argues. Conflict isn’t a sign that something is broken; it’s often a sign that two people care about something deeply. What shapes a relationship over time is less about avoiding fights and more about how you repair afterwards.

Repair can be small: a softened tone, a hand on the shoulder, an “I got defensive there.” It means pausing when things escalate, returning when you’re both calmer, and trying to understand the feeling underneath your partner’s words rather than only the words themselves.
If the same argument keeps coming back, couples therapy can help you slow the cycle down, see it clearly and build new ways of reaching for each other.

h1: How to know when it’s time to start therapy
h2: Gentle signs it might be time
h3: You don’t need a diagnosis to begin
p: There’s no perfect moment to begin. But there are a few gentle signs that talking to someone could help — here’s how to recognise them.
The Journal · Notes from our therapists

Many people wait for things to feel “bad enough” before reaching out. The truth is, therapy isn’t only for crisis. It can be a place to understand yourself better, untangle patterns that keep repeating, or simply have one hour a week that belongs entirely to you.

Maybe you’ve noticed that sleep, appetite or energy have shifted. Perhaps worries loop long after the moment has passed, or relationships feel more strained than usual. Sometimes it’s quieter than that — a sense of being stuck, flat or not quite yourself. Any of these are valid reasons to talk to someone.

A good first session is a conversation, not a test. You can arrive unsure of what to say, and your therapist will help you find the thread. If it feels useful, you keep going. If it doesn’t, that’s useful information too.

Today, our team works with individuals, couples, families and young people, in person and online. We’ve grown, but our heart hasn’t changed: every person who reaches out deserves warmth, honesty and care that fits their life.

You’ll always be met with warmth, honesty and respect — and you’ll always have a say in how your care unfolds.
